CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain retaliatory posture against List 3 tariffs while signaling conditional willingness to resume high-level talks. Do not escalate beyond measured retaliation, but do not concede under pressure — the asymmetry of the tariff war means China cannot match the US dollar-for-dollar, and further unilateral escalation from Beijing would only give Washington justification to go to $500B. Instead, file the WTO complaint, impose the announced $60B retaliation at graduated rates, and prepare domestic stimulus measures (fiscal easing, targeted monetary support) to cushion the export sector.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE:

Threat Score (+0.65): The threat to China is high and escalating rapidly. The US has already imposed $50B in tariffs (List 1 $34B effective July 6, List 2 $16B effective August 23), and the comment period for List 3 ($200B, potentially at 25% rather than 10%) closes on this very date, September 6. Bloomberg reports Trump wants to proceed as early as next week (Business Insider, Aug 30). Trump has threatened to "go to 500" — taxing all $505B of Chinese imports (NPR, Aug 23). The tariff asymmetry is severe: China has retaliated on all available US imports (~$130B) but cannot match further US escalation dollar-for-dollar (Politico, Aug 3). The yuan has depreciated ~7% against the dollar since April, testing the key 7.0 level (SCMP, Aug 11; NYT, July 24), signaling capital outflow pressure and currency stress. J.P. Morgan analysts warn that indirect effects on business sentiment and investment could cause 'large' collateral damage beyond the direct export hit (CNBC, July 18). China is simultaneously trying to manage financial deleveraging while supporting growth — a policy dilemma that the trade war makes much harder (CNBC). Former PBoC adviser Yu Yongding warned of potential capital outflow risks and currency depreciation spirals (SCMP, Aug 11). However, the threat is not yet existential: exports to the US account for roughly a fifth of China's total, and domestic demand + fiscal stimulus can partially offset the drag. The CCP's one-party system gives Xi Jinping advantages in managing domestic fallout — controlling media, directing fiscal response, and rallying nationalist sentiment (LA Times, Aug 3).

Action Score (-0.3): Retaliation is appropriate but must be calibrated. China has already announced $60B in retaliatory tariffs at graduated rates (5-25%) covering 5,207 categories (NYT, Aug 3; Politico, Aug 3). This is the maximum retaliation China can mount given the trade imbalance, and it has been described by the Commerce Ministry as 'rational and restrained' (Politico, Aug 3). Further escalation beyond this — such as non-tariff measures against US companies — risks triggering the full $500B tariff threat and would damage China's own investment climate and Made in China 2025 goals. However, conceding now would be strategically premature: Trump has said there is 'no time frame' for ending the dispute and does 'not anticipate much' from negotiations (NPR, Aug 23). Talks between lower-level officials in late August ended with only 'constructive and candid' language and no agreements (CNN, Aug 23). Concession without a matching US offer would signal weakness and invite further pressure. The right posture is to absorb the hit, retaliate proportionally, use WTO channels to build international coalitions, and focus domestic policy on cushioning the blow through fiscal stimulus and targeted monetary easing — as J.P. Morgan recommended (CNBC, July 18). This positions China for eventual negotiations from a stance of resilience rather than capitulation.
key_factors: List 3 ($200B) tariff imminent — comment period closes Sept 6, Trump reportedly wants to proceed next week
Tariff asymmetry: China can only retaliate on ~$130B of US imports vs $505B of Chinese exports to US
Yuan depreciated ~7% since April, approaching 7.0 threshold, capital outflow risk
Low-level talks in late August produced no agreements; Trump says 'no time frame' for resolution
US economy strong (consumer sentiment 100.1, industrial production rising) — reduces US incentive to compromise
China's dual challenge: deleveraging while supporting growth during trade war
WTO complaint filed — opportunity to build multilateral coalition against US unilateralism

sources_cited.excerpt: List 2 tariffs take effect: US 25% on ~$16B (completing the $50B package). China imposes matching ~$16B retaliation.
USTR publishes proposed List 3: ~$200B of Chinese imports for an additional 10% tariff (~6,000 product lines). Public comment / hearing process begins.
At Trump's direction, USTR says it is considering raising the proposed List 3 rate from 10% to 25%.
Trump reportedly wants to hit China with tariffs on $200 billion worth of goods... The tariffs could go into effect after the public-comment period ends on September 6.
Trump told Reuters there's 'no time frame' for ending the trade dispute, and that he doesn't 'anticipate much' from the trade negotiations in Washington.
China announced it would impose tariffs at four different rates (5%, 10%, 20%, 25%) on $60B of US goods... Beijing will be unable to match U.S. tariffs on a dollar-for-dollar basis.
Former PBoC adviser Yu Yongding warned the yuan would face downward pressure which may reinforce depreciation expectations, and China should be prepared for a new round of capital outflows.

J.P. Morgan analysts: indirect effects on business sentiment and investment could lead to 'large' collateral damage. Easing monetary conditions and allowing currency to absorb shock are the right policy choices.
Yuan depreciated ~7% against dollar since mid-April, testing 7.0 level. China managing deleveraging while trade war pressures growth.
